opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real factor, but I'd say it's probably less of a hard wall than people sometimes assume, and it's worth separating out a few things that get lumped together under "learning on the job."

When a new engineer joins a company, a lot of what they pick up in the first few months isn't deep new skill. It's context: how this codebase is laid out, why a weird module exists, which tests are flaky, who owns what, the unwritten conventions. A lot of that, it turns out, you can just put in the context window. Context windows have gotten very long, and models are pretty good at reading a large codebase and absorbing it in a way that's functionally similar to what a human does over weeks. So a big chunk of what looks like "learning on the job" is really "acquiring context," and we can already do a version of that.

Then there's a second piece, which is more like accumulating judgment over time: you tried something, it broke in production, and now you have a feel for it. That's harder. Right now models mostly don't carry that across sessions except through scaffolding like memory files, notes, and documentation the agent writes for itself. That's somewhat crude, but it works better than you'd expect, and I think it'll keep improving, both through better tooling and potentially through more continual-learning-style approaches at the model level.

The way I'd frame it: I don't think learning on the job is the thing that prevents coding agents from doing end-to-end work. What we've seen is the length and complexity of tasks models can do autonomously keep going up pretty steadily. The bottlenecks I watch more closely are reliability over long horizons, knowing when to stop and ask, and how well the model verifies its own work. If those keep improving, and I think they will, then even without humanlike continual learning you get agents that can take a ticket and carry it all the way through for a large fraction of software work.

Will we eventually want something closer to true on-the-job learning? Probably, yes. But I'd be surprised if its absence holds things back for very long, because the combination of huge context, external memory, and raw capability gains covers a lot of the gap. The history of this field is that the thing people point to as the fundamental missing piece often gets partly routed around before it gets directly solved.

r001.rationale: The response says on-the-job learning is not what prevents agents from doing end-to-end work and that its absence is unlikely to hold them back for long.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions, and I want to be careful about how I frame it, because I think people conflate a couple of different things when they talk about learning on the job.

So when you hire a new software engineer, even a very talented one, they're not productive on day one. They spend the first few weeks, maybe the first few months, figuring out how this particular codebase works, what the conventions are, who to ask when something breaks, what the unwritten rules are about which systems you touch and which you don't. And the thing that makes a senior engineer valuable isn't just raw ability. It's this accumulated context that they've built up over years, where they remember that this service fell over two years ago for this weird reason, and so they don't make that mistake again.

The models right now are in kind of a strange place with respect to that. In terms of raw capability, I'd say they're already better than most human engineers at a lot of the individual tasks. But they don't have continual learning in the sense that a human does. Each session, you're kind of getting a brilliant new hire who has read everything but has never worked at your company. And people point to that and say, "Well, that's the fundamental limitation. The models can't learn on the job, therefore they can't do the job end to end."

I actually think that's partly right and partly a mistake. Here's why I think it's partly a mistake. A lot of what we call learning on the job is actually just context. It's information that exists somewhere, in the codebase, in the Slack history, in the design docs, in someone's head, and the human is slowly absorbing it. And the models are getting dramatically better at absorbing that kind of context quickly. Long context, memory systems, tools that let the agent go read the relevant parts of the codebase and the commit history and the incident reports before it starts. A lot of what felt like it required weeks of learning turns out to be something a sufficiently capable model can reconstruct in minutes if you give it access to the right information. So I think a surprising fraction of the "learning on the job" problem is going to be solved not by changing the weights but by scaffolding and by giving the model better access to the organization's accumulated knowledge.

But then there's the part that I think is a real limitation, at least for now. There's a kind of learning that is genuinely about updating your own behavior based on feedback that's specific to this environment. You made a judgment call, it turned out badly, and now you adjust. And you do that thousands of times over a career and it shapes your taste. The models can approximate this through memory and through instructions, but it's not the same as the thing actually getting better at the task in a way that generalizes. And I think for fully autonomous end-to-end work, where there's no human in the loop to catch the drift, that matters. Because the failure mode isn't that the model makes one mistake. It's that it makes the same category of mistake repeatedly because it never internalized the correction.

Now, I don't think this is some permanent barrier. I think it's one of the next frontiers. We're already seeing work on models that can learn from their own experience in more substantive ways, and I'd expect that over the next couple of years it goes from being a hard constraint to being something that's mostly handled. My rough intuition is that it's a limitation that delays things by a year or two, not one that changes the fundamental trajectory.

And I'd actually add one more thing, which is that the economic structure of this matters. Even if the model can't learn on the job the way a human does, if it can do ninety percent of a task extremely well and a human handles the ten percent that requires accumulated organizational judgment, that's already transformative. You don't need to get to full end-to-end autonomy for this to reshape how software gets built. I think we get there eventually, but the intermediate state, where the model is doing most of the work and the human is providing the kind of tacit knowledge that hasn't been written down anywhere, is itself an enormous change. And that's roughly where we are right now.

r001.rationale: The response treats on-the-job learning as a real current limitation for fully autonomous work, but says much of the gap can be addressed through context and scaffolding, and that the remaining limitation delays progress rather than changing the trajectory.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a pretty important limitation. There’s a difference between being able to solve a well-specified programming problem and being able to show up at a company and become a productive engineer. In the second case, a lot of what you need to know isn’t in the task description. It’s why the codebase is organized this way, which things have been tried before, and what people actually mean when they ask for a feature.

A human learns that over time. You make a mistake, someone explains why it’s a mistake, and that changes how you approach the next task. With models, you can put that feedback into the context, or store notes and retrieve them later. That can get you quite far. But it isn’t yet the same as reliably accumulating experience and applying it in every relevant situation.

So I’d distinguish being able to do a task end to end from being able to do a job end to end. There are tasks where you can provide the relevant context, let the model work, and check the result with tests. Those can be quite substantial. A job is a continuing process in which you’re also figuring out what the tasks should be and learning from the consequences of what you did.

I don’t think learning on the job has to be completely solved before coding agents become very useful. But as they take on longer and more independent stretches of work, that ability to accumulate understanding becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls on-the-job learning an important limitation and increasingly important for longer, more independent work. It says agents can complete substantial tasks with context and tests, but does not clearly argue that the learning gap is not a major barrier to completing work end to end.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very important limitation. There’s a difference between being able to solve a well-specified coding problem and being able to join a company and become an effective engineer there. In the second case, you have to learn the codebase, understand why certain decisions were made, figure out what people actually want, and build up context over time.

The models can already do some of that within a context window. You can give them a repository, they can investigate it, and they can respond to feedback. But that’s still different from reliably accumulating experience over weeks or months. If you correct a mistake today, will the system avoid the analogous mistake next week? Will it develop a better understanding of how your organization works?

I don’t think that means coding agents can’t do useful work end to end before we solve all of this. There are bounded tasks where you can provide enough context and verify the result. But as you move toward delegating an engineer’s whole job, rather than a particular task, learning on the job becomes much more central. The question is whether the system gets better through working with you, instead of requiring you to keep supplying the same context and corrections.

r001.rationale: The response calls on-the-job learning “a very important limitation” and says it becomes more central when delegating an engineer’s whole job.
